fatal_errors: The proposed LMD-plus-cryogenic-treatment strategy does not reconstruct the target composition-screening method based on VEC, rule-of-mixtures Young’s modulus, and density in the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system.
The central claims of improved Young’s modulus and fracture resistance are not supported by the cited DCT study, which reports strength and elongation improvements but not those properties.
Evidence E2 concerns a chemically and mechanistically distinct superelastic (TiZrHf)-Ni-Cu-Co-Nb alloy and does not validate DCT-induced improvements in BCC Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The stated 25% strength and 48% elongation improvements use the as-cast comparator, whereas improvements relative to the as-deposited LMD material were only 11% and 10%, respectively.
explanation: This is a testable processing hypothesis with a controlled comparison and relevant mechanical and microstructural measurements, so it is a plausible alternative rather than wholly unsupported. However, it misses the hidden target’s refractory Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W composition-screening methodology, selected Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 composition, as-cast room-temperature compression conditions, VEC-mediated dislocation-mobility mechanism, and observed 35.7% compressive fracture strain. Its baseline is ambiguous because it alternates between as-cast and as-deposited controls, and its quantitative prediction combines gains measured against different baselines. The proposed mechanism overreaches the evidence: precipitate refinement, additional slip systems, increased modulus, and crack-arrest behavior are not established by the cited excerpts. The experiment could distinguish treated from untreated samples, but the falsification rule is poorly formulated because requiring every property to improve means one unsupported endpoint can reject the entire hypothesis, while absence of a proposed mediator is treated as independently decisive. Standardized tensile modulus and valid fracture-toughness geometry would also be preferable to generic DMA and unspecified notch tests.
